title: Tulsidas at Ram Ghat
hookLine: a poet waits by the river to see Rama, and pilgrims still walk barefoot around the hill
carry: keep the holy at the center
tomorrow: what does Rama tell Sita on the mountain?
last: GRIHA PRAVESHA: BLESS THE HOME, THEN ENTER.

cards: Most stories happen in places you can't go. Nobody can buy a ticket to Middle-earth.
But on the border of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh there's a small town called Chitrakoot, with a green hill, a river and a lot of temples.
Every day pilgrims arrive, take off their shoes, and start walking around the hill where, they believe, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana once lived in a hut of leaves.

teach.h: CHITRA AND KUTA: THE BRIGHT PEAK.
teach.b: Start with the name. Chitra means bright, many-colored; kuta means a peak. The bright peak.
Valmiki names its river, the Mandakini, and it still runs through the town, past the main bathing place, Ram Ghat. Now a story the town tells about itself.
The poet Tulsidas, who retold the Ramayana in Hindi, longed to see Rama with his own eyes. A well-loved tradition says Hanuman told him where to wait: Chitrakoot.
So he sat at Ram Ghat, grinding sandalwood paste for the pilgrims' foreheads.

teach.h: A BOY ASKS FOR SANDAL PASTE.
teach.b: A boy came and asked for a mark of sandal paste. Tulsidas handed it over and went back to work. He didn't look up.
In the telling, Hanuman, as a parrot in a tree, sang out a verse to wake him, and Tulsidas looked up into Rama's face. Tellings differ, but in many, Rama himself puts the mark on the poet's forehead.
The story carries a Hindu teaching: God can be standing right in front of you, at an ordinary riverbank, asking for something small.

That's why Hindus call some places tirthas, crossing places, where the holy has touched the earth. And they honor them by walking around them. Pilgrims circle Kamadgiri, the hill at the center of town, often barefoot.

teach.h: PARIKRAMA: THE HOLY ON YOUR RIGHT.
teach.b: This is parikrama, also called pradakshina: walking around something holy, keeping it on your right.

teach.h: KEEP THE HOLY AT THE CENTER.
teach.b: Many teachers explain it simply: God stays at the center, and your life moves around it. Hindus do the same in temples, circling the inner shrine. So the walk at Chitrakoot isn't sightseeing.
It's prayer with your feet. A picture of a whole life: everything moving, God at the center.

how: Pilgrims at Chitrakoot bathe at Ram Ghat on the Mandakini and walk the parikrama around Kamadgiri hill, often barefoot, keeping it on their right; in temples, worshippers circle the inner shrine the same way.

o: the city on the Sarayu where Rama was crowned king

the bright peak, now a pilgrim town with a hill to walk around

games.q: the holy town — tap the pairs.
p: a crossing place, where the holy touches earth
circling the holy, keeping it on your right

s: pilgrims circle the hill keeping it on their left
they keep it on their right, with the holy at the center.
Valmiki names the Mandakini river at Chitrakuta
and it still runs through the town today.
in the Tulsidas story, the poet knows Rama at once
he hands over the sandal paste without looking up, until a parrot's verse wakes him, in the telling.

games.q: you're a pilgrim at the foot of Kamadgiri hill. how do you honor it?
o: walk all the way around it, keeping it on your right.
games.why: pilgrims walk the parikrama around the hill, often barefoot, keeping it on their right: the holy at the center, their life moving around it.

practice: If you can, stand and walk slowly around something you hold holy: a home shrine, a tulsi plant, a small lamp. Keep it on your right, the way pilgrims circle Kamadgiri. One circle, or three.
If you don't pray, circle something you love, or simply turn once where you stand, and notice what sits at the center of your days.

wordCard.voice: Chitrakoot, today. A pilgrim town on the Mandakini, where Tulsidas is said to have seen Rama at Ram Ghat, and where people walk barefoot around Kamadgiri, keeping it on their right.

orig.note: Sanskrit citrakūṭa: the bright or many-colored peak, citra plus kūṭa; Chitrakoot in Hindi.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the holy at the center. That's what the walk around the hill means. See you tomorrow.
